newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Futures regulators begin patrolling the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Futures regulators begin patrolling the Internet.

text.p: Futures regulators are casting a probing eye at the Internet, which potentially offers huge new opportunities not just for investors but also for high-tech criminals.

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) now has "cybercops who roam the Internet on a daily basis, looking for financial crime with specially-appointed search engines," said John Tull, a CFTC commissioner, who was attending a futures industry conference here.

Tull said the CFTC is coordinating such efforts with other agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), to patrol home pages, investment-related chat rooms and other sites on the Internet looking for fraud and other violations.

So far, he said, the CFTC, as a result of its monitoring efforts, has brought enforcement actions against two people charged with offering computerized trading programs via the Internet without proper registration.
Part of the problem for regulators will be how to patrol a system with such a vast number of sites and a virtually unlimited number of users with global access.

"The Internet heightens the need for international cooperation to ensure the ability of any given jurisdiction to enforce its own laws without being frustrated from afar," said Tull. "It may be time for international regulators to come up with some type of agreed-upon gate-keeping or disclosure principles," he said. But he said there are difficulties associated with something so new.
"We are visiting with other regulators. We're going to have to feel our way through," Tull said.

Some executives of U.S. futures trading firms have worried privately about the implications of offering information on the net which could be called up in a country where a certain product might not be allowed.
In other cases, investors in countries where regulations are fairly tight with respect to conventional products may suddenly be confronted with new types of scams.

In Switzerland, for example, the investment newspaper Finanz und Wirtschaft reported that a firm with an internet site raised large sums of money from investors after touting development of technology about which scientists have expressed doubt.

Singapore regulates Internet providers, the firms which offer the link between users and the Internet. But Victor Liew, chairman of the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), conceded this did not block undesirable sites.
"People think you can control the Internet but you can only control the Internet providers," he said.
Privately, other executives said that anyone in Singapore, or anywhere else for that matter, could simply dial a provider in another country and access any site.
"You just have to dial up a provider in Australia or somewhere else," said one.
